source: Wang, Min, Deng, Shen, Wu, Zettlemoyer, Sun (2023) Towards Understanding Chain-of-Thought Prompting: An Empirical Study of What Matters
finding: Direct ablation of step order inside CoT demonstrations. Breaking step order (coherence) and relevance hurts a lot; logical validity matters little.
numbers: text-davinci-002, GSM8K answer acc: standard 15.4, CoT 48.5, invalid reasoning 39.5, no coherence (wrong order) 23.1, no relevance 11.0 (below standard). Bamboogle answer F1: CoT 45.2, invalid 39.4, no coherence 33.8, no relevance 23.9. Invalid reasoning keeps over 80-90% of CoT.
quote: Relevance to the query and correct order of steps are much more important
limits: Order is of steps inside a demonstrated rationale, not of Dewey-type stages. Old model, 800 GSM8K items. Nearest direct order ablation found.
agent_relevance: Order of steps is a real causal factor (GSM8K 48.5 to 23.1), but validity of each step is not. Supports keeping S-stage order coherent; says nothing yet about define/test stage order.

source: Chen, Chi, Wang, Zhou (2024) Premise Order Matters in Reasoning with Large Language Models
finding: Permuting the order of premises, with the task unchanged, drops accuracy a lot. Best when premise order matches the order of the proof.
numbers: Deductive reasoning: permuting premise order can cost over 30 points. GPT-4-turbo 96.5% at forward order (ratio 1) vs 82.0% at ratio 0 and 76.0% at 0.5. GPT-3.5-turbo and Gemini 1.0 Pro fall from over 65% to below 25%. R-GSM math benchmark also drops; GPT-4-turbo and PaLM 2-L lose up to 20-30 points in shuffle conditions.
quote: LLMs achieve the best performance when the premise order aligns with the context required in intermediate reasoning steps
limits: Premise order, not stage order. Models up to early 2024.
agent_relevance: Order effects are large in LLMs. Any S-stage ablation should log order and expect big effects; an agent that reorders evidence into proof order may gain.

source: Stechly, Valmeekam, Kambhampati (2024) On the Self-Verification Limitations of Large Language Models on Reasoning and Planning Tasks
finding: Equal-compute test of the review step: with a sound external verifier, re-sampling with the same prompt (no critique text) matches critique loops. LLM self-verification collapses.
numbers: GPT-4, 100 instances per domain. Game of 24: standard 5%, LLM+LLM critique 3%, sound verifier binary feedback 36%, first-error feedback 38%, resampling k=15 28%, k=25 42%, self-consistency over 15 6%. Blocksworld: standard 40%, LLM+LLM 55%, sound verifier 60/87/83%, resampling k=25 72%, self-consistency 42%. LLM as verifier on Game of 24: accuracy 87.0%, FPR 10.4%, FNR 20.7%.
quote: performance increases seem to stem in large part just from having enough guesses and a sound verifier
limits: GPT-4 (2024), three formal domains. Column mapping of Table 1 read from scrambled PDF text; graph colouring and Mystery Blocksworld show the same pattern at lower levels.
agent_relevance: Answers gaps 2 and 3 for non-reasoning models. A review stage pays for its tokens only if a sound check exists; with one, plain re-sampling plus the check is nearly as good as rich critique. Cheap gate = any executable or symbolic check.

source: Tyen, Mansoor, Carbune, Chen, Mak (2024) LLMs cannot find reasoning errors, but can correct them given the error location
finding: Splits review into finding the mistake and fixing it. Finding is the bottleneck. A location signal (oracle, or a small trained classifier) enables net-positive backtracking.
numbers: BIG-Bench Mistake, 2186 CoT traces from PaLM 2, 5 tasks. Best mistake finding, GPT-4 direct step-level: overall accuracy 52.87. With oracle location, backtracking nets a gain: a 50% base on tracking shuffled objects would become 68.6%, but a 99% base would fall to 92.8%. Random location is worse than oracle. Losses plateau at about 65% classifier accuracy. A small out-of-domain trained classifier (PaLM 2 Otter) beat 3-shot PaLM 2 Unicorn on 4 of 5 held-out tasks (e.g. Dyck +22.59, word sorting +11.66; one task -0.67; tracking and arithmetic rows not mapped reliably).
quote: LLMs cannot find reasoning errors, but can correct them given the error location
limits: Only 45 correct traces per task; 85/15 skewed sets; 2023-2024 models; per-task columns of Table 6 scrambled in the PDF text, so per-task gains are not recorded.
agent_relevance: Cheap gate for revision = an error-location signal, even imperfect (about 65% accurate). Revising an already-correct trace costs accuracy, so the gate must also say no error.

source: Tsui (2026, COLM) Self-Correction Bench: Uncovering and Addressing the Self-Correction Blind Spot in LLMs
finding: Models fix an injected error when it is in the user turn but not when the identical error sits in their own turn. Reasoning models do not show the gap. Appending Wait closes most of it for non-reasoning models.
numbers: 14 open non-reasoning models: average blind spot 64.5%. Claude 3.5 Haiku 52.5%, Sonnet 4 41.4%. Non-math logic and tracking 62.8%. Datasets: SCLI5 286, GSM8K-SC 1,313, PRM800K-SC 448 items. Appending Wait cuts the blind spot by 89.3%. Macro accuracy base / Wait / reasoning model: DeepSeek-V3-0324 0.567 / 0.902 / R1-0528 0.908; Qwen3-14B 0.117 / 0.868 / 0.843; Qwen3-32B 0.045 / 0.793 / 0.894. Fine-tuning on 5,306 correction traces cuts the blind spot 76.0%. On natural errors only 4.3-10.8% are caught when shown externally.
quote: Reasoning models exhibit a small, even negative, Self-Correction Blind Spot
limits: Injected errors are off-policy; temperature 0, 1,024-token budget; LLM judge (95.0% three-judge agreement on 238 samples).
agent_relevance: Answers gap 4: current reasoning models already do the back-step internally; for a non-reasoning base model a one-word re-entry cue gets nearly the same accuracy. An explicit review scaffold is largely redundant for reasoning models.

source: Gandhi, Chakravarthy, Singh, Lile, Goodman (2025, COLM) Cognitive Behaviors that Enable Self-Improving Reasoners
finding: Four behaviours (verification, backtracking, subgoal setting, backward chaining) predict whether a model gains from RL. Priming with them lifts a weak model; empty or padded thinking does not.
numbers: Countdown, RL: Qwen-2.5-3B reaches about 60% vs Llama-3.2-3B about 30%. Priming Llama with these behaviours matches Qwen. Empty chain-of-thought and length-matched placeholder thinking stay at 30-35%. Priming on incorrect solutions with the right behaviour patterns performed the same as correct solutions (Fig 6).
quote: the presence of reasoning behaviors, rather than correctness of answers, proves to be the critical factor
limits: One task (Countdown) for the main result, 3B models, RL training not a prompt scaffold. 200,000 pretraining documents sampled show these behaviours are rare.
agent_relevance: Dewey-like moves (check, back-step, decompose) are what use extra compute; tokens alone do not. Supports content-bearing stages in S1-S9, not extra length.

source: Yang et al. (2025) Dynamic Early Exit in Reasoning Models (DEER)
finding: Training-free stop rule: at reasoning-transition tokens, try an answer and stop if model confidence in it is high. Cuts length and often raises accuracy.
numbers: 11 reasoning models, 10 benchmarks: length cut 19.1% to 80.1%, accuracy change +0.3 to +5.0 points. R1-Distill-Qwen-7B overall 64.2 vanilla to 69.2 DEER at 61.5% of tokens. Qwen3-14B 82.8 to 83.7 at 57.1%. QwQ-32B 82.6 to 84.0 at 80.9%. Blunt NoThinking baseline loses accuracy: Qwen3-14B 66.9 at 34.1% tokens.
quote: consistently effective on 11 cutting-edge reasoning LLMs
limits: Math, science and code benchmarks; confidence from token probabilities; QwQ has unreliable end-of-thinking tokens.
agent_relevance: Answers gap 5: a confidence-gated trial answer at stage boundaries is a working stop rule for the test stage; blind truncation is worse.

source: Liu and Wang (2025) Answer Convergence as a Signal for Early Stopping in Reasoning
finding: Models usually reach their final answer after about 60% of the reasoning steps. Three stop rules tested: answer consistency, boosting end-of-thinking, and a trained probe (Learn-to-Stop).
numbers: Five benchmarks, five open models. Convergence typically after 60% of steps. Tokens cut over 40% on NaturalQuestions with answer consistency and accuracy up. Learn-to-Stop token cut 46.2% on NQ for R1-Qwen-7B, 47.7% for R1-Qwen-32B, 46.4% for R1-Llama-70B, 34.1% for the 8B. Unsupervised rules become unstable on MATH-500 and GPQA.
quote: models typically converge to their final answers after 60% of the reasoning steps
limits: Open distilled R1 models; the trained probe needs internal activations, unavailable for closed models.
agent_relevance: Answers gap 5: rule-based stop works on easy items, a learned stop is needed on hard ones. For an API agent the cheap rule is k repeated identical trial answers.

source: Chen et al. (2025) Do NOT Think That Much for 2+3=? On the Overthinking of o1-Like LLMs
finding: o1-like models spend far too many tokens on trivial items; the first solution is usually already right.
numbers: For 2+3 o1-like models used 1,953% more tokens than conventional models and gave 13 solutions. In more than 92% of cases the first round already contained the correct answer (QwQ and R1, ASDIV and MATH500, read from Fig 5). More solutions are produced on easier test sets (QwQ on ASDIV 3.5 on average).
quote: Subsequent solutions, which account for the majority of generated tokens
limits: QwQ-32B-Preview and R1-type models, late 2024. Mitigation (self-training) numbers not recorded. The 92% figure was read from a two-column PDF extract.
agent_relevance: Answers gap 5: stop after the first checked solution on easy items; extra rounds are mostly waste.

source: Li, Kim, Wang (2025) QuestBench: Can LLMs ask the right question to acquire information in reasoning tasks?
finding: Tests the define-the-problem stage on underspecified items. Models pick the right clarifying question easily in math but poorly in logic and planning.
numbers: Four sets: Logic-Q, Planning-Q, GSM-Q, GSME-Q. Models reach 40-50% on Logic-Q and Planning-Q, over 80% on GSM-Q and GSME-Q (GPT-4o zero-shot on the full sets: 99.39% GSME-Q, 84.05% GSM-Q). Chain of thought and few-shot gave no significant gain across models. Filtering to items where the model solved the well-specified version left Logic-Q unchanged and moved GSM-Q/GSME-Q accuracy by up to +39 or about -10 points.
quote: models struggle to identify the right question even when they can solve the fully specified version
limits: Multiple-choice clarifying-question selection, one missing variable only. Gemini 2.5 Pro shown only qualitatively. Per-model table scrambled.
agent_relevance: Answers gap 6: solving ability is not enough for a define stage. S1/S2 needs its own check of what is missing; a CoT prompt alone did not help.

source: Fan et al. (2025) Missing premise exacerbates overthinking (not re-read this session; relies on b22)
finding: Reasoning models on ill-posed items with missing premises produce long, unproductive reasoning instead of flagging the gap.
numbers: From b22 (opened by finder B): over 3,000 tokens on missing-premise items, as in K12.
limits: Not re-opened here, so opened is false.
agent_relevance: Same as K12: a define stage that must output premise-missing is a guardrail reasoning models do not supply by default.

source: Zheng et al. (2023) Judging LLM-as-a-Judge with MT-Bench and Chatbot Arena
finding: GPT-4 as judge agrees with human experts on answer preference about as well as humans agree with each other.
numbers: MT-bench non-tie setting: GPT-4 vs humans 85%, human vs human 81%. Humans found GPT-4 judgments reasonable in 75% of disagreements and changed their choice in 34%.
quote: over 80% agreement, the same level of agreement between humans
limits: Agreement on pairwise answer preference, not on process or stage adherence; the authors note position, verbosity and self-preference biases.
agent_relevance: Answers gap 8 only in part: judging final-answer preference is reliable, stage adherence is not shown. Peczuh's .54-.60 on CT essays is the more relevant figure.

source: Zheng, Zhang et al. (2025) ProcessBench: Identifying Process Errors in Mathematical Reasoning
finding: Locating the first wrong step in a solution is hard for prompted critic models and good only for the strongest reasoning models.
numbers: 3,400 cases with expert-annotated first-error step. Overall F1: o1-mini 87.9, GPT-4o-0806 61.9; best open model QwQ-32B-Preview competitive with GPT-4o but below o1-mini. Existing PRMs generalise poorly beyond GSM8K and MATH.
quote: QwQ-32B-Preview has demonstrated the critique capability competitive with the proprietary model GPT-4o
limits: Math only; step-level error location, not stage adherence. Table layout scrambled, so only the figure averages are recorded.
agent_relevance: Answers gap 8: a process judge needs a reasoning-class model (F1 88 vs 62). A cheap non-reasoning judge for stage scoring will be unreliable.

source: Snell, Lee, Xu, Kumar (2024) Scaling LLM Test-Time Compute Optimally can be More Effective than Scaling Model Parameters
finding: Equal-compute comparison of sequential revision vs parallel sampling on MATH. The best split depends on item difficulty.
numbers: Compute-optimal allocation beats best-of-N using about 4x less computation (revisions and PRM search). Easy items gain more from sequential revisions; hard items need parallel resampling or tree search. FLOPs-matched: a small model plus test-time compute can beat a 14x larger model on easy and intermediate questions, with little benefit on the hardest.
quote: effectiveness of different approaches to scaling test-time compute critically varies depending on the difficulty of the prompt
limits: PaLM 2-S*, MATH only; revision ability was fine-tuned in, not prompted.
agent_relevance: Answers gap 2: review (S9) pays on easy-to-medium items, independent samples on hard ones. A difficulty estimate should route between them.

source: Zhang et al. (2025) Understanding the Dark Side of LLMs' Intrinsic Self-Correction
finding: Intrinsic self-correction makes current models waver and overturn correct answers; prompts such as Are you sure bias them.
numbers: GPT-3.5-turbo changes 81.3% of answers more than 6 times in 10 rounds. Llama internal answers change at 14.1% per self-correction pass vs 8.3% in initial generation. One Llama-3.1-8B case shows a large accuracy drop with 58.8% of correct answers overturned. Mitigations: question repeating and small SFT.
quote: self-correction can fail across a range of tasks
limits: Table cell values scrambled in the text; only figures stated in prose recorded.
agent_relevance: Confirms K04 for newer models (Llama-3, DeepSeek, ChatGPT). A review stage needs a no-change option and a cue that is not you-are-wrong.

source: Kamoi et al. (2024) When Can LLMs Actually Correct Their Own Mistakes? A Critical Survey (re-checked for gap 10)
finding: Survey: no evidence that prompted self-correction works without reliable external feedback; works with reliable external feedback, with large-scale fine-tuning, or where verification is easier than generation.
numbers: Text-extracted this session; the CriticBench-style 41% base-accuracy threshold was not found, so gap 10 is not closed by this source.
agent_relevance: Same as K05/K06; supports gating review on a verifier.
